But if you go and be a nurse, you stay with it. You can't come home. You've got to graduate. And so she went training for nursing. She used to write home and say, oh, I can't take all these ballings off. Well, you take it. Other girls do. You take it and stay. Because you can't go home. Otherwise, I'll go. And you stay here and do the work. But she stayed and graduated. She was a wonderful nurse. She was a registered nurse.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: She married a fellow in Seattle. And of course, they were divorced. But she has five children. And her oldest, the grandchild, is a doctor now. And the other one is in medical school. He's going to be a doctor. So she did well.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: So you didn't try to become a nurse after that. Oh, no. I couldn't. I had to stay home.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: But the doctor, the in -genesis doctor, wanted me to become a nurse because he said, you've done such a good job taking care of your own family. And he said, I want you to be a nurse. But my sister, I don't want to be. She said, no, I want to be. I think I want to be a nurse. So I said, all right. You go on. You stay with it. Otherwise, you have to come home and do what I'm doing.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you find that you had to be strict when you were mothering the kids, bringing them up?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Not too bad. No. We got along just wonderful. If they didn't behave, I'd tell my dad.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: And he was strict. Yeah, you bet he was strict.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: He was strict. At the same time, he was a good father.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: You know, I've been told that by quite a few people.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Their fathers were pretty strict in those days. I think in those days. In older days, they were. More so than the mothers.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Your father being strict, did that mean that he punished the kids pretty easily?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: I can't think of anyone punishing him, hitting him or anything like that.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: They knew not to mind him. And I did too.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: He must have grown to depend on you a great deal when you took care of the house.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: In fact, he didn't want me to get married at all. He was selfish that way. But I took care of him after he had his stroke. I took care of him for five months before he died.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: He hated losing me.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Sure, I can understand why.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: But I'm not sorry. Yeah, I did it again.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: I guess that life was harder then, and you had to do what needed to be done to get by.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: He didn't live to be too old a man. He was just 64 when he died. Had a stroke and died. But he was awfully good to his mother, I tell you. She lived with us for 18 years.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did he have timber on the place? Was it easy for you to get your wood to burn for winter?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Oh, they used to go up to Troy and buy the cordwood every summer.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would they cut it or buy it?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: No, they'd buy it already cut. The cordwood already cut. And then they'd bring it home and saw it up. They'd split it from the stove and leave some chunks to the heating stove.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: So there was really no wood in the...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: There was no wood right handy around the vicinity?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Oh no, they had to go up near Troy to get cordwood.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about water? Was that easy for you to get where you lived?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Oh, we had water in the house.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: We had a well and a windmill and pumped on top of the hill. And then came back, had cold water in the house. Had a sink in the house with cold water, but not hot water.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you had a windmill?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Uh huh, I had a windmill.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did most of the neighbors have windmills then too?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: No, take my father. He'd have windmills, you know. He was the first one to have everything. He was the first one to have a hack, first one to have a buggy, first one to have a car, first one to have a windmill. And I don't know how he did it, but he did. Never in debt. Never. He never bought anything, but he paid for it.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: I wonder how it came about that he could even afford to, you know, to buy at all. I suppose it must have been the good crops that he had, the good land. Oh, he had good crops and good prices.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But a windmill now, is that really useful to have? Did it work well?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Sure, we had a wonderful well.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: It kept the cattle trough full of water all the time. We had a cistern on top of a hill, and it piped back down to the house, and it had a sink in the house with cold water. And then he, we had a bathroom that he fixed, and fixed corals in the cook stove on top of the range. We had hot water, we had baths, bathtub. There's a big sink bathtub.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did the other neighbors have, was water commonly easy to get in your neighborhood?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Oh, it was awfully easy to get water. It was. You didn't have to drop a well too deep or anything. No, I think they dug it by hand, you know. It wasn't too deep, but lots of water. Uh huh.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Yeah. Oh, it was really.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did many of the neighboring families, did many of them stay, or most of them stay when you were growing up? Was there, what I'm wondering is, was there much turnover of the farms?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: No, no, not, that's about the time, about the time that my father quit farming, but some of them quit farming, and moved to town. Some of them sold their place, the Rosner place was sold, the Duggar place was sold, but the Danielson's, they still stayed.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: And of course we sold our place to a fellow by the name of Berger, and he still has it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How old were you when your father passed away?

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: Twenty -eight.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: All the other kids had just about grown by then. Oh, they were all grown, all of them.

segments.speaker: Jennie Halverson Driscoll
segments.words: My youngest brother was, I think he must have been about twenty. Well, I will, I will get going, I can, it must be.
